articles.title: How to automate invoice processing without losing approval control
articles.article_format: Operational buyer guide with pass, review and stop control map
articles.target_client_type: Operationally complex UK SMEs with repeated supplier invoice entry, matching and approval work
articles.industry_or_operating_context: Broader UK SME finance and operations teams across ecommerce, wholesale, distribution, service and professional-services businesses

rolling_12_portfolio_mix_after_publicati.note: The published history remains ecommerce-led. This article continues the planned shift towards a 4 core / 8 broader balance in future rolling windows.

articles.primary_buyer_problem: Invoices arrive through email or uploads and staff repeatedly extract fields, check suppliers, match purchase orders, chase approvals and handle exceptions.
articles.primary_search_intent: Learn how to automate invoice processing while retaining financial approval and exception controls.
related_query_family: invoice processing automation for small business
articles.trend_or_durable_demand: Current regulatory and durable operational demand. UK policy is moving towards mandatory VAT e-invoicing from 2029, while current HMRC guidance already requires VAT records and specified digital links across software used for VAT records.
articles.evidence_source_and_date: HMRC and Department for Business and Trade e-invoicing consultation response, updated 26 November 2025; HMRC VAT record-keeping guidance checked 27 July 2026; HMRC Making Tax Digital for Income Tax guidance updated 16 July 2026.
articles.what_changed_or_matters: UK businesses have time before mandatory VAT e-invoicing, but invoice data, approvals, supplier checks and digital records need to be controlled before a mandate or software purchase forces a rushed process redesign.
articles.existing_article_gap: The site covered Shopify payout reconciliation, wholesale order entry and system hand-offs, but did not explain supplier invoice capture, purchase-order matching, approval limits and bank-detail exceptions as one controlled process.
articles.henry_distinct_contribution: A process and control view: automate evidence collection and repeatable checks before automating approval, and force uncertain invoices into a reason-coded review queue.

rolling_12_article_audit.why_distinct: The article addresses supplier invoice intake, OCR or parsing, duplicate tests, supplier verification, purchase-order matching, approval limits and bank-detail controls. It does not reconcile sales payouts, enter customer orders, compare system architecture or validate product listings.

articles.original_editorial_asset: A five-row invoice pass, review and stop control map covering supplier status, duplicate invoice numbers, purchase-order matching, bank-detail changes and approval limits.
articles.first_hand_contribution_or_limits: Uses Henry Oliver's proven process-design, data and control perspective. It does not claim first-hand accounts-payable experience in industries not stated.
articles.proof_points_used_recently: The 200,000-SKU and eight-hours-to-two-minutes proof points were not reused.
articles.readability_check: Passed editorial review for short sentences, active voice, plain British English and an intended Hemingway grade of 9 or lower.
articles.mobile_check: Passed conceptual checks at about 390px and 768px. The control table collapses into labelled single-column rows and the CTA remains fluid.
articles.ai_mention_check: Passed. AI is not presented as the offer. OCR is named only as one extraction mechanism.

quality_rules: Write for operationally complex UK SMEs while retaining ecommerce and wholesale as the strongest proof base.
Every article must read at Hemingway grade 9 or lower.
Do not invent results, statistics, dates, names or testimonials.
Every article needs distinct intent and at least one original editorial asset.
AI is one controlled tool, never the offer or a replacement for judgement.
